assumptions.context: How to thread the caller's `AbortSignal` reason from setupTimers into MultipartAbortError without library-side synthesis (F-S-006)
assumptions.choice: setupTimers reads `callerSignal.reason` at the moment of fire (in onCallerAbort) AND at the moment of already-aborted detection. The MultipartAbortError constructor takes the reason as its first arg. Because Sprint 1's MultipartAbortError stores `reason` as a readonly instance field WITHOUT embedding it into the message (the message is a fixed 'multipart: operation aborted'), the caller-supplied reason flows through without ever appearing in any library-generated string. Verified by the 'library does NOT embed source bytes / URL / headers into reason' integration test.
alternatives_considered: Wrap the reason in a library-defined Error subclass (rejected — F-S-006 forbids library-derived reason synthesis; the caller's reason MUST surface verbatim, not wrapped)
Store both signal.reason and a derived 'cause' chain (rejected — the data-model.md spec for MultipartAbortError defines exactly one reason slot; adding cause would require a spec amendment)

assumptions.context: How to implement the FR-009 already-aborted contract — the 'reject synchronously' part. Async generators cannot truly throw at construction time (per Sprint 3's existing T-002/T-003/T-025 contract — every throw surfaces from the first `.next()`)
assumptions.choice: Sprint 4 mirrors Sprint 3's existing pattern: validatePositiveTimeout throws inside the generator body (surfaces from first .next()), and the FR-009 already-aborted check immediately after setupTimers also throws by pushing the abort error into the queue (queue.signalError) — the for-await loop's `item.type === 'error'` branch then throws on first iteration. Either path produces identical caller-observable behavior: the first `.next()` rejects.
alternatives_considered: Throw synchronously from a non-generator wrapper that constructs the iterator only after validation passes (rejected — would change the public function shape from `function*` to `function` returning `AsyncIterable`, which is a breaking type-level change Sprint 4 should not make)
Add a custom 'aborted' check before the for-await loop (rejected — the queue.signalError approach is shorter and unifies the abort path with the mid-stream abort path)

assumptions.context: The combined-signal handler attached AFTER setupTimers — when does it fire? Could it race with the already-aborted-at-call-time check?
assumptions.choice: Two cases: (a) caller signal already aborted at call time → setupTimers' constructor-time check stores the error AND aborts the controller AND DOES NOT install the abort listener on the caller signal (the controller signal is already aborted, so adding a listener that calls abortInternally would no-op). The combined-signal listener attached after setupTimers tests `if (!timers.signal.aborted)` BEFORE adding itself — so it skips when already-aborted, avoiding double-listener. The synchronous queue.signalError(abortErr) in the already-aborted branch handles surfacing. (b) caller signal aborts AFTER call time → setupTimers' onCallerAbort listener fires, abortInternally stores the error and aborts the controller. The combined-signal listener (registered with `{ once: true }`) fires once and pushes the discriminated error into the queue. The `abortPushed` boolean prevents the unlikely but possible double-push from racing internal cleanup with the listener.
alternatives_considered: Have setupTimers' abortInternally directly call queue.signalError (rejected — couples Layer C/internal/timers.ts to the queue-notifier interface, breaking the architecture.md §3 'Layer C MUST NOT import from Layer A or B' rule)
Use a Promise.race shape between a TimerState.aborted promise and the queue.next() promise (rejected — adds a microtask hop and conflicts with Sprint 2/3's queue-driven dispatch model)

assumptions.context: Fake-timer fixture for idle/total tests — the brief lists `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ['setTimeout', 'clearTimeout'] })` plus a slowReadable, but advanceTimersByTimeAsync interleaving with Readable flowing mode can be tricky
assumptions.choice: Used a custom Readable whose `read()` schedules each chunk's push via setTimeout(callback, gapMs). With faked timers, `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(N)` releases setTimeouts in order, which lets `read()` push the chunk → parseMultipartRelated's 'data' listener fires → `timers.resetIdle()` is called. For idle-stall tests, the fixture is parameterized with `endAfterChunks=false` so when `chunks` are exhausted the source stays open silently (no `push(null)`) — this models a hung connection. Without that flag, `Readable.from(buf)` would push end-of-stream and we'd hit MultipartTruncatedError instead of MultipartIdleTimeoutError.
alternatives_considered: Lower-level EventEmitter shim simulating a Readable (rejected — Node Readable's pause/resume backpressure semantics are nontrivial to mock and would risk diverging from real-world behavior)

Use `Readable.from(asyncIterable)` with `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, gapMs))` (rejected — async generators driven by faked timers have an extra microtask hop that makes timing assertions brittle)
Real timers + `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, real_ms))` (rejected — would make the tests slow and flaky on shared CI)

assumptions.context: The slowReadable's `endAfterChunks=true` default vs the per-test override. Default behavior: Readable.from(buf) ends after pushing the buffer, so a normal multipart parse succeeds
assumptions.choice: Default `true` matches the most common test shape (slow-but-steady chunks → success). Idle-stall test (T-009) and total-timeout test (T-011) explicitly pass `endAfterChunks=false` because their contract is 'source never ends; timer must fire'. Captured in the fixture's JSDoc.

assumptions.context: T-046 race test: making both abort and idle fire in the same fake-timer macrotask
assumptions.choice: Schedule the abort via `setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort('race'), 1100)` while the idle window is `1000ms` (so idle's setTimeout fires at t=1100ms via the test's slowReadable's first chunk arriving at t=100ms). When `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2000)` runs, both setTimeouts (idle-fire at t=1100, abort-trigger at t=1100) are released in arbitrary order. The test asserts: (a) exactly ONE of MultipartIdleTimeoutError or MultipartAbortError surfaces (proves first-fire-wins); (b) cleanup invariants hold (source destroyed, listeners cleaned). The test does NOT assert WHICH class wins because the order is timing-dependent — first-fire-wins is the contract, not which-fires-first.
alternatives_considered: Force a deterministic winner via micro-mocking the AbortController (rejected — the test would no longer exercise the real race, defeating the point of T-046)
Run the test 100 times to check both winners are observed (rejected — adds flakiness and CI runtime; the contract is symmetric so verifying ONE side is sufficient)

assumptions.context: Sprint 4 brief says T-026b should test the cross-product (only one of the two timeouts supplied). I implemented this as 5 sub-tests in one describe block
assumptions.choice: Sub-tests: (a) Response overload missing idleTimeoutMs, (b) Response overload missing totalTimeoutMs, (c) Readable overload missing both, (d) Readable overload missing idleTimeoutMs only, (e) Readable overload missing totalTimeoutMs only, (f) invalid timeout values (T-060..T-065 surface). Each test uses an `as ParseMultipartOptions` cast to launder the static type error so the runtime check is exercised in isolation. Comment block in the describe explains why: the static FR-006 contract is enforced at compile time by ParseMultipartOptions's required-fields shape; the integration tests focus on RUNTIME enforcement for callers who bypass the type system.
alternatives_considered: Use `@ts-expect-error` directives on each call (rejected — the lint rule requires descriptions, and several of the call sites had directives that became 'unused' as the TypeScript type-check landed elsewhere; the cast approach is cleaner and lint-clean)
Use `// @ts-ignore` with no description (rejected — codebase forbids @ts-ignore and reasons about every static-type override)

assumptions.context: Where to place the FR-009 already-aborted check inside parseMultipartRelated. The brief says 'caller must check this in parseMultipartRelated BEFORE the for-await loop starts'
assumptions.choice: Placed RIGHT AFTER setupTimers and BEFORE the dicer/source listeners are attached. Rationale: setupTimers already detects the already-aborted state and records it; we just need to surface it as a queue error so the for-await loop's first iteration throws. Doing it before listener attachment is technically not required (the timers won't fire because they're not armed when already-aborted), but doing it here keeps the early-return shape close to the validation pattern Sprint 3 established (validate, set up state, pre-pipe listeners, pipe).
alternatives_considered: Throw the abort error directly from the generator body (rejected — would skip the cleanup() call in the iterator's finally; the queue.signalError + iterator-loop-throw shape goes through the same finally-driven cleanup as every other error path)

assumptions.context: The exactOptionalPropertyTypes constraint on calling setupTimers with `signal: opts.signal`. Sprint 1 set `signal?: AbortSignal | undefined` on ParseMultipartOptions, but exactOptionalPropertyTypes means I can't pass `{ signal: undefined }` to a function whose parameter is `signal?: AbortSignal | undefined`
assumptions.choice: Used the conditional spread shape `...(opts.signal !== undefined ? { signal: opts.signal } : {})` so the property is OMITTED when undefined rather than included with an undefined value. This pattern is consistent with how Sprint 2's parseMultipartRelated handles the optional contentId/contentLength fields on StreamingMultipartPart (line 246 of parse-multipart-related.ts).
alternatives_considered: Loosen TimerStateOptions.signal to `AbortSignal | undefined` non-optional (rejected — would force every internal caller to explicitly pass `undefined`, less ergonomic and a regression of the NFR-DR-A-013-style internal-types-MAY-be-bare-optional rule)

assumptions.context: Sprint 4's MultipartIdleTimeoutError construction in setupTimers. The brief example uses `new MultipartIdleTimeoutError({ idleTimeoutMs, elapsedMs })` (object-arg) but Sprint 1's actual constructor signature is `new MultipartIdleTimeoutError(idleTimeoutMs, options?)` (positional)
assumptions.choice: Followed Sprint 1's actual constructor signature (positional first arg) — the brief's example was illustrative, not the literal API. Same for MultipartTotalTimeoutError. Verified Sprint 1's signature in src/errors.ts before implementing. The error fields (`idleTimeoutMs`, `totalTimeoutMs`) are still set as readonly instance properties exactly as the brief expects, just via the positional constructor.
alternatives_considered: Modify Sprint 1's error classes to take an object info-bag (rejected — Sprint 4 brief explicitly says 'src/errors.ts: all 7 classes exist with their structured fields from Sprint 1. Just import + throw' — modifying error classes is out of scope)

assumptions.context: T-046 race test's assertion 'exactly one of MultipartIdleTimeoutError or MultipartAbortError surfaces'. The first-fire is timing-dependent under fake timers — could produce inconsistent results across vitest versions
assumptions.choice: Assert the disjunction `captured instanceof MultipartIdleTimeoutError || captured instanceof MultipartAbortError === true`. This captures the contract (first-fire-wins; cleanup is idempotent) without binding to which side wins on this particular vitest+Node combination. The 'cleanup is idempotent' invariant is asserted via the listener-leak harness (source.destroyed, dicer listener counts, partStream.destroyed). If first-fire-wins ever broke (e.g. a future implementation accidentally surfaces BOTH errors), the test would fail because `captured` would be the second-fire which has no instanceof match.
alternatives_considered: Use process.nextTick + manual re-ordering to force a specific winner (rejected — defeats the purpose of T-046, which is to verify the contract under genuine racing)
Run the test in a loop and count both winners observed (rejected — adds flakiness and runtime; symmetric contract means one side is sufficient)

assumptions.context: validate-timeout.ts: the assertion-function shape `asserts value is number`. TypeScript will narrow the value type AFTER the call returns. But `value` is typed as `unknown` to handle the missing-required-field case
assumptions.choice: Implemented as `asserts value is number`. Caller pattern: `validatePositiveTimeout('idleTimeoutMs', opts.idleTimeoutMs)`. After the call, `opts.idleTimeoutMs` is guaranteed to be a valid number. Inside the function body, `value` is narrowed to number after each successful check via the `||` short-circuit. The implementation order matters: `typeof value !== 'number'` MUST be the first check to prevent runtime errors from `Number.isFinite(undefined)` etc.
alternatives_considered: Return a narrowed number value rather than asserting (rejected — would force callers to re-bind `opts.idleTimeoutMs = validatePositiveTimeout(...)`, more ceremony for no benefit)
